parts.title: Our village goes green
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Four years ago, our village decided to make all its own electricity. At the time, many people laughed. We live in a valley in the hills, far from any city, and most houses used oil to keep warm.

The first step was to put solar panels on the roof of the village hall. They worked so well that the hall now makes more electricity than it needs. Then a farmer, Mr Brook, built a small wind turbine in his field. At first the neighbours complained about the noise, but now they say they hardly hear it.

The next idea was the river. A small machine in the water uses the current to make power day and night. It cost a lot of money, but the villagers paid for it together, and each family owns a small part.

Today, we sell some of our extra electricity to the city and use the money to repair the school. My little sister says that we are the greenest village in the country. I think she may be right, and I am proud of it.

questions.prompt: Why did people laugh at the idea?
options: The village is small and far away
The weather there is often cloudy
The river was too wide to use
The village had no school or shop
questions.explanation: They lived in a valley far from any city.

questions.prompt: What happened with the village hall?
options: It needed a new roof last year
It closed for repairs in summer
It makes more power than it needs
It was built by Mr Brook
questions.explanation: The hall makes more electricity than it needs.

questions.prompt: What did the neighbours say about the turbine?
options: It is far too tall for them
It spoils the view of the hills
questions.explanation: They now say they hardly hear it.

questions.prompt: How was the river machine paid for?
questions.explanation: The villagers paid for it together.

questions.prompt: What is done with the extra electricity?
options: It is sold to the city
It is given to the school
questions.explanation: They sell some to the city and use the money to repair the school.

parts.title: Where does our electricity come from?
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Every time we switch on a light, electricity flows to the bulb. But how does it get there? [1] Most of it is made in big power stations far away from our homes.

For many years, power stations burned coal, oil or gas. [2] This is bad for the planet, because it sends dirty gases into the air.

Today, more and more countries are changing to clean energy. The wind, the sun and moving water never run out. [3] Some countries now make half of their electricity in this way.

But there are problems. The sun does not shine at night, and the wind does not always blow. [4] This is why scientists are working on better batteries.

What can we do? [5] Switching off lights, using less hot water and walking short distances all make a difference.
sentences: The system of wires that carries it is called the grid.
Thomas Edison built one of the first of them in New York in 1882.
We therefore need ways to store energy for later use.
This kind of fuel will not last for ever.
Small actions by ordinary people add up to a big change.
The idea is not new, but it has become cheaper in recent years.
Nobody knows exactly when it was invented.
Some people say that these machines are too ugly.

gaps.explanation: The grid is the system of wires that carries electricity, answering how it gets there.
This kind of fuel will not last for ever; the next sentence says it is bad for the planet.
The idea is not new but cheaper recently, and the next sentence says some countries make half their power this way.
We need ways to store energy, which leads to better batteries.
Small actions add up, and the next sentence gives examples.

parts.title: A message about the electricity bill
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Hi Dad, I hope you are well. I wanted to tell you that our electricity bill came yesterday, and it was much higher [1] usual. Mum thinks that it is because we [2] the heating on all day last month. I have promised to turn it off when I leave the house. Also, my brother always leaves his computer [3] all night. I have told him to stop, but he does not listen. If this carries on, we [4] have to pay more than we can afford. Do you think that we should put solar panels [5] the roof? Grandpa says they are expensive, but they would save us money in the [6] run. Let me know what you think. Love, Evie

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: Higher than usual: a comparison.

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: Had the heating on all day: past simple of have-on.

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: Leaves his computer on: switched on.

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: If this carries on, we will have to pay: first conditional.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: On the roof: the preposition for a surface.

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: In the long run is a fixed phrase.

parts.title: The first electric light
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Before electricity, people used candles and oil lamps to see in the dark. They did not give much light, and they were often dangerous, [1] a small fire could burn a whole house. In the nineteenth century, scientists started to look [2] a safer way to light our homes. The man who is most famous for this is Thomas Edison, an American inventor. In 1879, he made a light bulb that burned for more [3] thirteen hours. Many people had tried before him, [4] they had failed. It took Edison and his team thousands of experiments to find the right material. Soon, cities began to build power stations, and electric light became part [5] everyday life. Today, we use light bulbs that need much less power, [6] they last for years. It is hard to imagine a world without them.

gaps.explanation: Dangerous because a small fire could burn a house: a reason.
Look for a safer way: phrasal verb look for.
More than thirteen hours: a comparison.
Many had tried, but they had failed: contrast.
Part of everyday life: a fixed phrase.
Need less power, and they last for years.

parts.title: Short conversations
parts.instructions: Listen to seven short conversations. Choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Hello, this is Martin from Northside Electric with a message for customers on Pine Road. Many of you called this morning because the power went off at about six. First, every bill on the road is paid, so nobody will lose their power. Some people also thought that a street lamp had blown and caused the problem. One of our workers checked it, and the lamp was fine. In fact, the wind and rain last night were so strong that a tree fell on the main cable at the end of the road. After the storm, our team went out at dawn, and they are working there now. We expect the power to be back by lunchtime. Thank you for being patient.

question.explanation: The bills are paid and the street lamp was fine; the wind and rain of the storm knocked a tree onto the main cable.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Is that a brochure for fridges, Marco? Yours still works, doesn’t it?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: It works fine, yes. But it’s twenty years old, and my electricity bill has gone up again.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: So you want a bigger one? You always say it’s too small when the whole family comes for Christmas.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I do say that, but it’s only a few days a year, and I don’t need more space. The shop assistant showed me a silver one and a bright red one. The red one is lovely, but I don’t mind about colour.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Then what’s the point of changing it?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: The new ones are very efficient. I read that I would pay a third less every month.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Well, that’s sensible. Is it expensive?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: More than I wanted, but it pays for itself.

question.prompt: Why will the man buy a new fridge?
question.explanation: He says the fridge still works, that Christmas is only a few days and that colour does not matter; he reads that a new one would cost a third less in electricity.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Welcome to Greenfield town centre. If you drive an electric car, you can charge it for free this month. The old charging point outside the station closed last year, and some visitors still look for it there, but please don’t. People also ask about the cinema, where there is a plan for a new charging point, but the building work doesn’t start until next spring. At the moment, the only place is the new car park behind the supermarket, next to the recycling bins. It has six places and it is open all night. Please remember to bring your own cable, because we don’t lend them. Thank you, and enjoy your visit.

question.prompt: Where is the charging point for electric cars?
question.explanation: The station point closed last year and the cinema point is only a plan for next spring, so the only place is the car park behind the supermarket.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: How was the science fair, Finn? Did your little brother win anything?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: He got second place! He’s only twelve.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Wow. Did he make that solar oven he was talking about in the summer?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That was his first idea, actually. But the weather was bad all August, so it never got hot enough, and he gave up on it.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Oh no. And the battery? Somebody told me about a battery project.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That was his friend Leo, who did that one. My brother built a little model from plastic bottles and an old bicycle motor. When you blow on the blades, like the wind does, a tiny bulb comes on.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: That’s clever!

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: He’s very proud of it. He wants to build a bigger one next year.

question.explanation: The solar oven was his first idea but he gave up, and Leo made the battery; the brother made a model with blades and a motor, which is a wind turbine.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Do you still cycle to college every day, Emma?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Most days, yes. I used to take the car on dark evenings, but I bought better lights for my bike, so now it doesn’t bother me.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: And what about when it’s freezing? You hate the cold.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I wear thick gloves. I only took the car once or twice in the winter, and that was when I woke up very late and had to hurry.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: So you never go by car?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Only when there’s heavy rain. My bag, my books and my laptop get wet, and it isn’t worth it. Then Dad drives me.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That sounds sensible.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Yes, and he never complains, because the college is on his way to work.

question.prompt: When does the girl go to college by car?
options: When it is cold and dark
question.explanation: She cycles in the dark with good lights, wears gloves in the cold and only once took the car when late; she goes by car when the rain is heavy.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Many phone batteries run down before lunchtime. Many people blame phone calls, but a call uses very little power. Others think that the camera is the problem. It does use some power, especially with the flash, but one photo only takes a second. The real problem is on the screen. When you play games, the picture is bright and moves all the time, and the phone works hard. One hour of playing can use a quarter of your battery. So here is my tip: put a time limit on your games, make the screen a little darker, and you will get home with some power left.

question.prompt: What makes the phone battery run down quickly?
question.explanation: Calls use little power and a photo only takes a second; the bright, moving picture of games works the phone hard.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: It’s so hot in here. How do I turn on the fan?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: There’s a button on the fan itself, but it’s easier with the wall switch.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Is that the one next to the window? I can see a switch there.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: No, that one is for the blind. And the one above the sink is for the extractor, which is a different thing and makes a terrible noise.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: So where’s the one for the fan?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: It’s in the same place as the light, where you came into the room.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Oh, I see it now. I’d never have found it.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Everybody says that.

question.prompt: Where is the switch for the fan?
options: On the wall by the door
question.explanation: The window switch is for the blind and the sink switch for the extractor; the fan switch is where the light switch is, at the entrance.

turns.speaker: f

turns.speaker: f

They would make his house ugly
They are a good plan for the long term
question.explanation: The price scared him at first and he does not care about looks, but he has done the sums and will get his money back in nine years.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: My toaster is making a funny smell. I think I’ll keep using it. It’s only a bit of smoke.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: A bit of smoke? Please don’t. Switch it off at the wall and pull out the plug.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: But it only needs cleaning. I could take it apart and wash it.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I wouldn’t. The wires are probably old and it could catch fire. Don’t take the risk.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: A new one costs thirty pounds, though. I hate wasting money on something that still works.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Honestly, I’d rather spend thirty pounds than lose my kitchen. My brother tried to repair his, and no shop would touch it afterwards.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: OK, you’ve convinced me.

question.prompt: What does the woman think about the old toaster?
question.explanation: She tells him to switch it off, says the wires are old and could catch fire, and prefers to pay for a new one, so she thinks it is dangerous.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Did you hear? Our school team won the energy prize!

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Really? I voted for the other school, because I thought their idea was better. But the judges chose ours.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Are you disappointed? You’ve been helping them for months.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Not at all. To be honest, I didn’t expect them to win with that idea, but they worked so hard all term. Of course the prize money of a thousand pounds is nice, and I won’t pretend that I wouldn’t like it.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I guess.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: But I’m not jealous. When I saw the team hold up the cup, I couldn’t stop smiling. I felt so proud, it was a real success. And I’m not tired of the project either. I’d start again tomorrow.

question.prompt: How does the man feel about the school team?
question.explanation: He is not disappointed or jealous of the money and wants to start again, and he cannot stop smiling when the team wins, so he is proud.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Freya, have you ever been to the wind farm on the hill? I’m thinking of going on Saturday.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Once. Is it for your geography project? I remember you have to write about energy.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That’s due in November, so there’s lots of time. No, the school has a photo contest, and the theme is "Our region". I think the turbines against the sunset would make a great picture.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Isn’t it a bit far? Your uncle works near there, doesn’t he?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: He does, but I’ve seen his office many times, and it’s boring. I just want to take the best photos before the sun goes down.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Then go early, because the buses are slow on Saturdays.

question.prompt: Why does the boy want to visit the wind farm?
options: To take photos for a contest
To get ideas for a school project
To see where his uncle works
question.explanation: The project is due in November and he has seen his uncle’s office many times; he wants good pictures of the turbines for the school contest.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Finn, I walked past the gym at eleven last night and all the lights were still on.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Again? That must cost a fortune. Shall we write to the head teacher?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: She’d say she’s too busy. And she’d send us to the caretaker anyway.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: True. What about changing the bulbs? The LED ones use much less power.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: They do, but they cost a lot, and the school has no money this year. Only the caretaker has the keys and the switch. If he turned the lights off when he locks up, it would solve the problem for free.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: You’re right. I’ll catch him tomorrow after school. He’s always in the boiler room at four.

question.prompt: What do the two friends agree to do about the gym lights?
options: Write a letter to the head teacher
Change the bulbs for new ones
Ask the caretaker to switch them off
question.explanation: A letter would be passed to the caretaker and new bulbs are too expensive, so they agree that the caretaker should turn them off when he locks up.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: You look worried, Felix. Is it the essay?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: No, it’s finished and saved. I even put a copy online. And the screen is fine, I bought a strong case for it last week.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: So what’s wrong?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: My battery is at five per cent, and I left the charger at my cousin’s house. We have the presentation in the morning and I need the laptop for the slides.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Can’t you borrow one?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Not easily. The plug is a different shape from the normal ones. I’m just afraid that it will run out of power in the middle of the talk.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I think mine might fit. I’ll look tonight.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Please do. You’re a lifesaver.

question.prompt: What is the boy worried about?
question.explanation: The essay is saved and the screen is protected; what worries him is that the battery will die during the presentation because he has no charger.

parts.title: A talk about a wind farm
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: nathalie
turns.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Hill Top Wind Farm. My name is Fiona, and I’m one of the engineers here. Before we walk up the hill, let me tell you a few things. The idea was born about ten years ago, when the council started to look for clean energy, but for a long time nothing happened. Building started eight years ago, and the farm opened six years ago, which is quite fast for a project of this size. Originally, we planned twenty-four turbines, but some neighbours complained, so there are twenty of them today. You can see them on the ridge behind me. Each one is taller than you think. The tower alone is sixty metres, but when you add the blades, the whole thing reaches eighty metres, as high as a twenty-storey building. Now, the question that most people ask: how much power do we make? Last year the farm produced enough electricity for fifteen thousand homes. The year before, it was only nine thousand, because there was less wind and one turbine was being repaired. Many visitors imagine that summer is our best season, and it’s true that we get lovely days then. But the wind is strongest in winter, and that is when we make the most power. Autumn comes second, with storms, but sometimes they are too strong, and then we have to stop the turbines for safety. Finally, a word about our visit. There is a path from here to the top. The full circle takes two hours, but today we’ll take the short route, which takes about one hour, and that includes a break at the viewpoint. Please wear strong shoes, because the ground is wet. If you have questions, ask me on the way. Shall we go?

gaps.prompt: The farm started to work ___ years ago
gaps.explanation: Building started eight years ago and the farm opened six years ago; the idea was ten years ago.
Twenty-four were planned, but because of complaints there are twenty.

gaps.prompt: Counting the blades, a turbine reaches ___ metres
gaps.explanation: The tower alone is sixty metres; with the blades the total is eighty.

gaps.prompt: Last year the farm supplied ___ homes with electricity
gaps.explanation: Last year fifteen thousand homes; the year before it was nine thousand.
Summer has lovely days and autumn has storms that are too strong, but the wind is strongest in winter.
The full circle takes two hours, but the short route is about one hour.

parts.title: An interview with an electrician
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Fabian, how did you become an electrician?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Well, my father was one, and people always think I just followed him. He did take me to jobs at the weekend, and I enjoyed it. But honestly, that wasn’t the main thing. I’ll admit that the money is decent, though a few of my friends earn more in offices. What really got me was the first time I fixed a fault by myself. It was a bedroom where nothing worked, and after two hours I found a loose wire. It felt like solving a puzzle, and I wanted that feeling every day.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What kind of work do you do now?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: In the past I mostly fixed sockets and lights, and sometimes I helped on building sites with new houses, but builders have their own teams for that now. I do paint a wall after I put in new cables, to leave the room tidy, but I always say it’s not my job. The big change is the sun. Every month more families ask me to put panels on their roof and connect them to the house, and it keeps me very busy.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Is there a golden rule for safety?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Always cut the power before you touch anything, and check it with a tester. Rubber gloves are useful, and I wear them for some jobs, but they aren’t the first thing, because a glove can have a hole. A good partner is useful too. I sometimes work with my apprentice, but even alone I follow the rule, even when I’m in a hurry.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Tell me about a strange problem that you solved.

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Last winter a woman called me because her lights flickered every evening. She had changed all the bulbs, even though they were new. Everybody thought it was the storm, because it began after a big one, but the wiring in the house was fine. In the end, I looked in the loft and found a cable with teeth marks. A mouse had chewed it. She laughed and said she would have preferred a storm.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: How long does it take to learn the job?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Some people think a one-year course is enough. You can learn the basics, yes, but you won’t be safe. Others tell me about ten years, which is the time to become a real expert. That’s true for me, but nobody needs it to start. The usual way is about four years: college, training with a company and then an exam.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What would you say to a teenager who wants to do it?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Study mathematics. Some people say history is useful because you learn to read long documents, and others say music helps your ear for the job, but that’s nonsense. The real reason is the numbers. You calculate how much power a cable can take and how long a cable you need. I do these sums every day. It isn’t easy for everybody, I know, but it pays off.

questions.prompt: Why did Fabian choose his job?
options: He wanted to earn a lot
questions.explanation: His father was an electrician and the money is decent, but the main thing was the feeling of solving a puzzle by himself.

questions.prompt: What does Fabian do more and more often?
questions.explanation: Builders have their own teams and painting is not his job; more families ask him to put panels on the roof.

questions.prompt: What is the first rule of safety?
questions.explanation: Gloves and a partner are useful but not first; he always cuts the power before touching anything.

questions.prompt: What caused the flickering lights?
questions.explanation: The bulbs were new and the wiring was fine despite the storm; a mouse had chewed a cable in the loft.

questions.prompt: How long does it take to learn the job?
questions.explanation: One year gives only the basics and ten years makes an expert; the usual way is about four years.

questions.prompt: Why does Fabian advise teenagers to study mathematics?
options: It helps with calculations at work
It teaches you to read documents
It improves your ear for music
questions.explanation: History and music are not the reason; he does sums every day to know how much power a cable takes and how long it must be.
